lead: SI and CI engines run the same four strokes but start the burning differently. An SI (spark ignition) engine mixes petrol with air first, compresses the mixture and lights it with a spark. A CI (compression ignition) engine compresses air alone until it is hot, then sprays diesel into it, and the fuel ignites by itself. That one difference sets the compression ratio, the way load is controlled, the weight, the efficiency and the exhaust, and so decides why scooters and cars burn petrol while trucks, tractors and gensets burn diesel.
prereq: You need the four strokes from four-stroke and two-stroke engines and the compression ratio from engine terminology and components.

sections.h3: SI engine: the mixture is made before it is compressed

blocks.text: Petrol is volatile, so it is mixed with air before it reaches the cylinder: in a carburettor, by an injector in the inlet port, or (in direct-injection engines) early in the intake stroke. The cylinder therefore holds a ready mixture when compression starts.

items: Intake: the piston draws in mixture; a throttle valve in the inlet sets how much.
Compression to a ratio of about 8 to 12; pressure and temperature rise, but the mixture must not ignite by itself.
Ignition: the spark plug fires 10° to 40° before TDC, because the flame front needs a few milliseconds to cross the chamber. The pressure peaks just after TDC.

blocks.text: If the compression ratio is too high, the last part of the mixture (the end gas) is heated by compression and by the advancing flame until it ignites all at once before the flame reaches it. This is knock; it limits the compression ratio of an SI engine, and petrol is rated by its octane number, its resistance to knock. Knock is taught in the unit on combustion.

Load is controlled by the throttle, that is by the quantity of mixture, whose strength stays near the chemically correct ratio. At part load the nearly closed throttle makes the piston suck against a partial vacuum, and this pumping loss is why a petrol car is thirsty in slow city traffic.

sections.h3: CI engine: air is compressed, fuel is injected at the end

blocks.text: There is no spark plug and, usually, no throttle. The intake draws in air only, and a compression ratio of about 16 to 22 heats it. With ideal compression from 300 K, a ratio of 18 gives about 950 K; diesel fuel ignites by itself in air above roughly 250 °C (about 520 K), so the air is far hotter than it needs to be.

Near the end of compression an injector sprays diesel at high pressure as fine droplets. They evaporate, mix with the hot air and, after a short ignition delay of about a millisecond, ignite at many points at once; the rest burns as fast as it mixes. Injection starts about 5° to 25° before TDC.

Load is controlled by the amount of fuel injected, with the air flow almost the same at every load. This is quality control: the mixture strength changes, and there is almost no throttling loss. Diesel is rated by its cetane number, its readiness to ignite, the opposite of what petrol needs.

The high compression ratio gives a CI engine its better efficiency, but also peak pressures far above those of an SI engine (modern diesels exceed 150 bar), so the block, head, rods and bearings are heavier, and the engine runs at lower speed. Ideal cycles for both engines are compared in ideal air-standard cycles.

head: Feature
SI engine
CI engine
rows: Diesel or dual (heat added at constant pressure, or both)
carburettor or injector before the cylinder
injection pump and injector into the cylinder
lower: heavier moving parts and slower burning
higher: high r and no throttling
CO and HC at rich mixture; NOx

blocks.text: Their exhausts need different treatment. An SI engine runs at the chemically correct mixture, so a three-way catalyst can clean CO, HC and NOx together. A CI engine always runs with excess air, so its CO and HC are low but its NOx and soot need their own after-treatment, taught in the unit on emissions.

examples.question: An SI engine has a compression ratio of 9 and a CI engine a ratio of 18. Both start compression with air at 1 bar and 300 K. Assuming ideal (isentropic) compression with γ = 1.4, find the temperature and pressure at the end of compression in each.
steps: For isentropic compression T₂ = T₁ r<sup>γ−1</sup> and p₂ = p₁ r<sup>γ</sup>.
Check: the CI air is 231 K hotter and at 2.6 times the pressure; both changes make diesel fuel ignite much sooner.
examples.answer: SI: 722 K and 21.7 bar. CI: 953 K and 57.2 bar. Real compression loses heat to the walls, so actual values are somewhat lower.

examples.question: A four-cylinder CI engine has a bore of 10 cm, a stroke of 12 cm and a compression ratio of 19. Find the clearance volume of one cylinder.
steps: Swept volume of one cylinder: V<sub>s</sub> = 0.7854 × 10² × 12 = 942.5 cm³.
V<sub>c</sub> = 52.4 cm³. The number of cylinders does not enter, because bore, stroke and r are all per cylinder.

traps: A CI engine compresses air only. Writing that it compresses a fuel-air mixture is the commonest error.
The injector and the spark plug are not interchangeable: one creates the mixture in hot air, the other lights a mixture already made.
A higher compression ratio is not always better: in SI it brings knock, in CI it brings higher peak pressure, heavier parts and more NOx.
Quantity control belongs to SI (throttle), quality control to CI (fuel quantity). Swapping the two words is a classic slip.
Octane measures resistance to self-ignition and cetane measures readiness to self-ignite. A good petrol is a poor diesel fuel and the other way round.

quiz.q: In which engine does fuel enter before the compression stroke begins?
quiz.a: The SI engine: the mixture is made in the carburettor or inlet port, or early in the intake stroke.

quiz.q: State the usual compression ratio ranges of SI and CI engines.
quiz.a: SI: about 8 to 12. CI: about 16 to 22.

quiz.q: Why does a CI engine not need a throttle to control load?
quiz.a: Load is set by the amount of fuel injected into an unchanged air charge, so the mixture strength changes instead of the quantity. With no throttle there is almost no pumping loss at part load.

quiz.q: Why is the SI compression ratio held below about 12?
quiz.a: The charge is premixed. A higher ratio heats the end gas until it self-ignites ahead of the flame, which is knock.

quiz.q: An engine has a swept volume of 900 cm³ and a compression ratio of 19. Find its clearance volume.
An engine has V<sub>c</sub> = 40 cm³ and V<sub>s</sub> = 600 cm³. Find r and say which type it probably is.
A mechanic plans to run a petrol engine of compression ratio 9 on diesel by fitting an injector in place of the spark plug. Give two reasons it fails.
quiz.a: First, temperature alone is not enough: the first worked example gives about 722 K, already above the 520 K self-ignition figure, but ignition delay falls steeply with temperature and pressure. A standard delay correlation (Wolfer’s) gives about 7 ms at 722 K and 21.7 bar, about 130°CA at 3000 rev/min, against about 0.5 ms at 953 K and 57 bar; with real wall heat loss the fuel burns very late or not at all and leaves as smoke. Second, the engine has no high-pressure injection system, its parts are not built for diesel pressures, and its throttle would starve it of air.

quiz.q: A diesel bus and a petrol car work in the same stop-start traffic. Which suffers more from part-load pumping loss, and why?
quiz.a: The petrol car: its throttle is nearly closed at part load, so the piston sucks against a vacuum every intake stroke. The unthrottled diesel sets load by fuel quantity, so its pumping loss stays small.

beyond: Petrol engines now often inject fuel straight into the cylinder at 200 to 350 bar, and diesels inject at 1500 to 2500 bar from a common rail, so the hardware difference has narrowed. Low-temperature modes such as HCCI try to auto-ignite a premixed charge with no spark at all, and gasoline compression ignition runs petrol in a diesel-like way. Search for gasoline compression ignition, spark-assisted compression ignition and common rail injection.
